text:
Gov. Bill Lee has signed into law a measure to punish judges in Tennessee who do not cooperate with federal immigration authorities.

The legislation, brought by Rep. Rick Scarbrough of Oak Ridge and Sen. Paul Rose of Covington — both Republicans — instructs each court to cooperate with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and federal immigration authorities, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Under the new law, a judge who “obstructs lawful operations” by these officials may now be referred to the state’s judicial oversight board for misconduct proceedings and, ultimately, removed from office, the legislation says.

The legislation does not define what actions taken by a judge would be considered obstructive and the bill’s sponsors skirted questions during the legislative session about whether the legislation was brought to address an identified problem.

ICE’s latest focus in Tennessee: traffic court

“I can’t speak to a specific event, but I’d like to consider here that this is a proactive bill,” Scarbrough said. “Nothing is more disruptive or embarrassing for any kind of agency than when you find you don’t have a policy to address a certain situation that has occurred…when those policies are nonexistent your practice becomes a policy.”

ICE agents in recent months have made periodic mass arrests of individuals showing up to answer summons’ for traffic and misdemeanor citations in Roberton and Wilson County. County court officials have declined to respond to questions by the Tennessee Lookout in the wake of these arrests about any agreements or cooperation between judges and immigration officials to secure the arrests.

A spokesperson for the Administrative Office of the Courts, which manages state court operations and often speaks on behalf of the Tennessee judicial system, declined to comment on the legislation.

The bill hit a roadblock late in the legislative session when the Tennessee Senate tried to soften the language. Ultimately, a compromise creating a Feb, 1 2029 expiration date for the law, secured its passage.

title: Congressman Greg Casar presses for release of Austin high school senior held by ICE
description:
AUSTIN, Texas — A Northeast Austin high school community is continue to rally around one of its students after federal immigration authorities detained the student during a traffic stop earlier this month.
Congressman Greg Casar (D-TX 35) is now getting involved and is calling for Cabrera's release.
He joined friends and supporters of Cabrera for a press conference on Monday morning outside of Northeast Early College High School, where Cabrera is senior.
“He is sitting in an ICE detention center for no reason other than a routine traffic stop,” Casar said.
He should be about to graduate,” Casar said.
text:
AUSTIN, Texas — A Northeast Austin high school community is continue to rally around one of its students after federal immigration authorities detained the student during a traffic stop earlier this month. That student was set to graduate in about three weeks.

Eighteen year old Luis Fernando Cabrera was driving home from his late-night shift at Popeyes around 2 a.m. on May 1 when a Texas State Trooper pulled him over along IH-35 in Austin for expired registration.

During the traffic stop, DPS said the trooper was unable to verify the driver’s identity through DPS databases, but “through further investigation,” the trooper determined he was “not lawfully present in the United States.” DPS contacted Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and turned him over to federal immigration authorities.

The Trooper who made the stop is a federally certified Delegated Immigration Officer under the 287g program. In October 2025, DPS signed 287 (g) agreements with ICE, which allow trained officers to be authorized by ICE to help enforce federal immigration laws while they are out on patrol.

According to government records, he is now being held at the Karnes County Immigration Processing Center, which is located Southeast of San Antonio.

Congressman Greg Casar (D-TX 35) is now getting involved and is calling for Cabrera's release. He joined friends and supporters of Cabrera for a press conference on Monday morning outside of Northeast Early College High School, where Cabrera is senior.

“He is sitting in an ICE detention center for no reason other than a routine traffic stop,” Casar said. “Donald Trump said he was going after the worst of the worst. Fernando is the best of us.”

The high school senior has lived in the U.S. since he was 11, when his family came to the U.S. from Mexico. A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Cabrara illegally entered the U.S. on July 28, 2019, near Eagle Pass, Texas.

“His family is from Honduras, but the persecution there, the situation was so bad that they embarked on that journey knowing that the mom was pregnant,” Luis’ attorney, James Harrington, said. “This was very dangerous, but they had no choice.”

Harrington said Luis had claimed asylum, and his case was still in the legal process.

“That doesn't seem to apply much to the administration these days in terms of who they arrest and jail,” Harrington said.

Since he came in as a minor, Harrington said his parents made the application and everything, and up until his 18th birthday in February, his parents were obligated to do all the necessary reporting, which he said they did.

“This is not unusual,” Harrington said. “This goes on all the time. People who are in process get deported.”

Casar stood next to Cabrera's cap and gown and said the 18-year-old should be getting ready to put them on, not sitting in a detention facility.

“Fernando is the kind of son we would all be proud to have, the kind of brother we would all be glad to have, the kind of community member we should all want to have. He should be home right now. He should be about to graduate,” Casar said. “These are the graduation robes that he's supposed to be wearing just days from now, and that's why we are demanding that Fernando immediately be released so that he can graduate from high school, so that he can be with his family and continue his life here in Austin, Texas.”

Cabrera's loved ones say he planned to attend Austin Community College after graduation.

They said he also played soccer and worked between 20 and 40 hours a week to help his family pay the bills.

“What more do we want in terms of a respectful person who's doing the best that he can, who was brought here by his family and is doing the best that he can?” Harrington added. “You can't find many more people in this school who have done what he has done to support his family and to get ahead in life.”

Harrington has known Luis since he came to the U.S.

“I've watched him grow, and this is the kind of kid that I would be proud of to have as a son,” Harrington said. “He is not a criminal. This is the furthest person from being a criminal that you can imagine.”

Harrington said Luis is “doing really well” and is appreciative of all of the support he has gotten, describing him as “pretty upbeat for somebody” who is “that young in that condition. “

During a rally by friends and family to support him last week, he called his sister and spoke with all his soccer friends.

“That's who Luis is, man. He's got that resiliency,” Harrington said. “I just hope in three weeks he is here wearing that robe.”

In a statement read by Casar, Luis’ sister called what happened to him cruel -- saying he is a good member of society who supported his family.

“He was a good soccer player. He had lots of friends. He had no problems with the law,” Holi said. “I don't understand why it's so important for ICE to jail people like my brother, who are good members of society who support their families.”

Holi described Luis as a “wonderful brother,” who works hard to support the family and is a good uncle to her two-year-old son, with whom he played with daily.

“Now that ICE has put my brother in jail, my baby walks into his room and only asks about his friend,” Holi said.

His loved ones said he had been so excited about graduations that he had his gown and printed invitations, and he showed them off to everyone at church the Sunday before he was arrested.

“He actually had all his credits and everything. He was a pretty smart person. It's very sad to see,” Juan Carlos Coronado Gonzalez, who has been friends with Luis for the last three years, said. “You wouldn't know how excited he was. We would always talk about it, and it is just sad to see that we're just going off without him, maybe.”

Throughout high school, Juan Carlos said Luis became more than a great friend. He considers him more like a family member.

“I'm just waiting for him to come out because we have so many great things to do, graduate and live through more memories that we have to live at school,” Juan Carlos said. “We have two more weeks, and he's supposed to be here with us while we're preparing for graduation, and he won't be here for us, but we're here for him to show him our support.”

Juan Carlos said Luis was always there for others, so now it's his friends' turn to be there for him, who's stuck in a cell hundreds of miles away.

“He was a friend that you always wanted,” Juan Carlos said. “To see him so far away and you can't even talk to him right now, it's just heartbreaking.”

In a statement, the U.S Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said Luis will remain in custody “pending immigration proceedings” and “will receive full due process.”

In its statement, DHS said, “Being in detention is a choice,” and encouraged those without proper documentation to remain in the United States to self-deport through the CBP Home App. The United States is offering those in the country illegally $2,600 and a free flight.

“We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream,” DHS said. “If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.”

Cabrera’s lawyers have filed a writ of habeas corpus appeal, arguing he does not need to be detained while his case plays out.

“We know from his conduct and what he's done to support his family and to graduate, he's not a flight risk, so there's no reason to detain him,” Harrington said.

Casar made a plea to anyone listening.

“Set your politics aside for a second and think of your kid being 18 years old, sitting in a jail cell for no reason, denied his ability to graduate, ripped away from his family and his friends and his community,” Casar said. “He was working. Imagine it's your kid who's working the late shift to help you and your family out, and then he is sent to a jail cell, God knows where, and your kid has done nothing wrong. Whether you voted for Donald Trump or not, I don't think anybody voted for this.”

This all comes as we have seen a sharp escalation in immigration enforcement activity over the last year and a half since President Donald Trump returned to the White House. Casar made a point of saying that Cabrera is one of many young people, not just in Austin but across the country, who federal authorities have swept up.

“Luis Fernando is as American as anybody else, just happened to be born somewhere else, but just like millions of people before him, his family fled violence and danger, and he came here of no choice of his own. But his parents made a brave choice, and he is going through the legal process that millions of people have gone through in the past to be able to stay here,” Casar said. “This administration, the Trump administration, has decided to arrest and detain and threaten with deportation people with no criminal record and pose no danger at all.”

He said what is different about this case is that Cabrera and his family are speaking up.

“There are so many more where families are afraid to speak up. This is just one of so many here across Austin, and across Texas, thousands of kids have been locked up,” Casar said. “It's just really important for us to fight here, for Luis Fernando to be able to get out, graduate, and be able to stay here. But then, for people to know that he is just one of so many children who have been arrested and locked up for just no good reason, that I think anybody could support.”

title: France: UN torture prevention body to make first visit to places of detention | OHCHR
description:
States are under the obligation to allow the SPT unannounced and unhindered visits to all places where persons are deprived of their liberty.
States Parties should also establish a national preventive mechanism, which should conduct regular visits to places throughout the country where people are deprived of liberty.
To date, the SPT has conducted more than 100 visits to countries that have ratified this Protocol.
However, States parties are encouraged to request that the SPT publish the reports.
The SPT is composed of 25 independent and impartial members who are independent human rights experts drawn from around the world, who serve in their personal capacity and not as representatives of States Parties.
text:
For media inquiries or for more information, please contact

In France: Bardia JEBELI, +41 79-444 4552 / bardia.jebeli@un.org

In Geneva: Vivian Kwok at vivian.kwok@un.org

UN Human Rights Office Media Section at ohchr-media@un.org

Background

To date, the Optional Protocol to the Convention Against Torture has been ratified by 96 states. States are under the obligation to allow the SPT unannounced and unhindered visits to all places where persons are deprived of their liberty. States Parties should also establish a national preventive mechanism, which should conduct regular visits to places throughout the country where people are deprived of liberty.

The mandate of the SPT is to prevent torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment of persons deprived of their liberty, through visits and recommendations to States parties to the Optional Protocol. To date, the SPT has conducted more than 100 visits to countries that have ratified this Protocol. The SPT communicates its recommendations and observations to States by means of a confidential report and, where necessary, to national preventive mechanisms. However, States parties are encouraged to request that the SPT publish the reports.

The SPT is composed of 25 independent and impartial members who are independent human rights experts drawn from around the world, who serve in their personal capacity and not as representatives of States Parties.

title: Minnesota Senate approves bills to regulate ICE officers after immigration surge
description:
“The way ICE agents and Border Patrol agents went about (immigration) enforcement was an absolute abuse of our Constitution.
It just crossed so many constitutional lines.” The Minnesota Senate is controlled by Democrats, who have made Operation Metro Surge recovery and accountability a top issue.
The Trump administration has said that federal agents have “absolute immunity” if they are conducting immigration enforcement.
It also prohibits federal immigration agents from schools, hospitals, childcare centers and courthouses.
States cannot regulate immigration law, and Republicans argue the bill package does just that.
text:
The Minnesota Senate on Monday approved a package of bills aimed at reining in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers after more than 3,000 federal agents descended on Minnesota for what the Department of Homeland Security called its largest immigration enforcement operation ever.

Swarming groups of federal agents racially profiled and arrested people in the streets during Operation Metro Surge, which ignited massive resistance and resulted in the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, two U.S. Citizens.

“All we want are safe communities and the fair treatment under the law,” said Sen. Ron Latz, DFL-St. Louis Park, and chief author of the bill package. “The way ICE agents and Border Patrol agents went about (immigration) enforcement was an absolute abuse of our Constitution. It contravened our constitutional principles. It was without warrants. It was stopping people without lawful basis. It was arresting people without probable cause. It just crossed so many constitutional lines.”

The Minnesota Senate is controlled by Democrats, who have made Operation Metro Surge recovery and accountability a top issue. The Minnesota House is deadlocked between Republicans and Democrats, and Republicans have largely opposed Operation Metro Surge-related bills this session. The legislative session ends on Sunday.

The bill passed 34-33 in the Senate with no Republican votes.

The package includes a bill to allow Minnesotans to sue federal agents in state court if their constitutional rights are violated.

For much of American history, people have had the ability to sue federal agents, but the U.S. Supreme Court has rolled back that precedent. The high court has suggested that only Congress can authorize lawsuits seeking money from federal officials.

Some legal scholars believe state legislatures, too, can authorize lawsuits against federal officials for violating the Constitution. The Illinois Legislature last year passed such a law, and the Trump administration promptly sued, arguing the Constitution’s supremacy clause limits states from enacting policies that conflict with federal law.

The Trump administration has said that federal agents have “absolute immunity” if they are conducting immigration enforcement. Legal experts say that immunity doesn’t extend to unreasonable or excessive use of force. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty charged one ICE officer with assault for allegedly brandishing a weapon and is weighing charges against the agents who killed Pretti and Good.

The package of bills also includes banning law enforcement from wearing face masks, and it creates a “civil right of action” in shootings in which a person can be held civilly liable if they shoot someone and fail to provide aid to the victim.

It also prohibits federal immigration agents from schools, hospitals, childcare centers and courthouses.

Senate Republicans say the package would cost taxpayers hundreds of thousands of dollars in potential litigation because the state will likely be sued. States cannot regulate immigration law, and Republicans argue the bill package does just that.

name: Policy
title: The economic chilling effect of Trump's immigration crackdown - VPM
description:
So, did the immigration crackdown help the job prospects of U.S.-born workers?
"Before 2025, ICE arrests were mostly not arrests in the usual sense of the word," the authors of the Deportation Data Project report write.
In 2025 and early 2026, the Trump administration doubled those traditional types of ICE arrests (aka transfers of custody).
There's a classic argument against immigration: that immigrants take jobs from U.S.-born workers or drive down wages.
And, research suggests, "employers are not able or willing to raise wages in order to attract U.S.-born workers to take those jobs."
text:
Shortly after Inauguration Day in 2025, Planet Money visited Little Village, a predominantly Mexican-American neighborhood in Chicago. It felt oddly quiet for what was usually a bustling part of the city, almost like a ghost town.

The Trump administration had signaled it was about to do big ICE raids there (and eventually did). Many in the community seemed to be scared to go about business as usual. There seemed to be a clear "chilling effect" on their economic activity — like going to work, shopping, eating out, and so on.

For that episode, we spoke with Chloe East, an economist at the University of Colorado Boulder, who has done extensive research on the economic effects of deportations. But back then, the only way to gauge the potential fallout from the second Trump administration's immigration crackdown was to look at past deportation efforts.

Well, we now have data from last year's immigration crackdown. East and a co-author, Elizabeth Cox, recently released a new working paper, "Labor Market Impacts of ICE Activity in Trump 2.0," which analyzes how Trump's beefed up immigration enforcement affected employment, both for immigrants and workers born in the United States. So, did the immigration crackdown help the job prospects of U.S.-born workers? East says no.

" The mass deportations in Trump 2.0 are not helping the labor market overall and not creating more job opportunities for U.S.-born workers," East says. In fact, she and her co-author find evidence that, if anything, the clampdown has hurt the employment prospects of U.S.-born workers, particularly working-class men who work in industries that are heavily reliant on undocumented workers, like construction.

It's more evidence that the labor market isn't really a zero-sum contest, where immigrants and native workers battle over a fixed number of jobs in a kind of labor market Hunger Games, and the newcomers take the jobs of or undercut the people already here. Instead, it adds to a large and growing body of evidence that, actually, immigration helps grow core industries and the overall economy, which creates jobs and has other benefits for native workers. Less of a Hunger Games, and more like… what's the opposite of a Hunger Games… a potluck?

How Trump 2.0 transformed immigration enforcement

One of the crucial datasets East relies on in her paper — national immigration enforcement under the second Trump administration — is accessible because of the work of a nonprofit called the Deportation Data Project.

The Deportation Data Project, which was founded by a political scientist and two lawyers, has successfully obtained immigration enforcement data through the Freedom of Information Act, enabling researchers like East to crunch it.

Before we get into the economic impact, it's worth getting into the data on immigration enforcement itself. The Deportation Data Project recently published an analysis of the data they've obtained, to see what happened during the first year of the second Trump administration.

They found that, after President Trump took office in January 2025, arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) more than quadrupled.

But the Trump administration did more than just increase the total number of arrests. It also transformed how these arrests are carried out. Federal authorities began enforcing immigration laws much deeper in the interior of the nation, as opposed to its more traditional zone near the border. And, the authors write, they dramatically increased the number of "street arrests," or community arrests, in neighborhoods, worksites, immigration courts, and check-in appointments at ICE offices.

"Before 2025, ICE arrests were mostly not arrests in the usual sense of the word," the authors of the Deportation Data Project report write. "Instead, they were transfers of custody from jails or prisons. In such transfers, noncitizens who were initially arrested on criminal charges (typically unrelated to immigration law), are moved by ICE to immigration detention facilities, where they are held for civil violations of immigration law." The Obama administration, for instance, relied heavily on these types of arrests, where undocumented immigrants are transferred from jails and prisons to ICE custody and then deported.

In 2025 and early 2026, the Trump administration doubled those traditional types of ICE arrests (aka transfers of custody). More dramatically, however, the Trump administration increased community (or "street") arrests by more than elevenfold, which, the authors point out, "explains why ICE street arrests seem like a new phenomenon."

With a large increase in community arrests, the Trump administration also ramped up arresting noncitizens without criminal records. The authors find there was an "eightfold" increase in arrests of noncitizens without a criminal conviction.

" ICE activity in the second Trump administration is the most indiscriminate it's been in the modern era," East says. "To immigrants living in our country, it has felt like leaving your house for any reason could cause an interaction with ICE, and could cause you to get arrested and potentially deported."

And that has real economic consequences. Because it's not just the physical removal of immigrants from communities that affects the economy. In fact, East says, the larger economic effect comes from the fact that the undocumented immigrants who remain here have been scared to go about business as usual.

East has found this "chilling effect" during mass deportation efforts in the past, including under the Obama administration. But, she says, it's loomed larger during the Trump administration, and it has been the driver of the negative economic outcomes that she and her co-author find in their new study.

The economic fallout

In her new study, East, together with University of Colorado Boulder economist Elizabeth Cox, takes this immigration enforcement data from the Deportation Data Project and combines it with economic data from the U.S. Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics to provide what they call "the first national, causal empirical evidence on the labor market impacts of immigration enforcement in the second Trump administration."

Their methodology is pretty simple. To isolate the effect of immigration enforcement on the labor market — from the gazillion other things affecting it — the economists take advantage of the fact that the Trump administration didn't enforce immigration laws everywhere equally. In what's known as a "difference-in-differences" approach, the economists basically compare places where the Trump administration vigorously enforced immigration laws to places where they didn't, and then see how workers in these areas fared over time (specifically, the first nine months of the administration).

The economists focus on two groups of workers, both aged 20 to 64. The first is workers born in the United States. The second is workers who they classify as "likely undocumented," namely "foreign-born individuals with at most a high school degree or equivalent who work in sectors where undocumented workers are over-represented." They further break down these groups by sex and educational attainment.

For likely undocumented workers who remained in the U.S., the economists find "a meaningful chilling effect" in which they reduce their employment by "a significant 4%." They find this effect is driven by men, "who make up over 90% of those arrested by ICE in our time period."

The economists then turn to U.S.-born workers. "And we find that for U.S.-born workers, overall there are no positive effects on employment or wages, and that actually for U.S.-born workers who are in the sectors that are most heavily reliant on undocumented workers — that they are harmed as a result of increased ICE activity," East says.

The U.S.-born workers most negatively affected, the economists find, seem to be men with "at most a high-school education" who work in sectors that rely on undocumented labor and were hit the hardest by ICE arrests and deportations.

" We find that for every six fewer undocumented workers working in a local labor market, that there is one fewer U.S.-born worker working in that labor market," East says.

There's a classic argument against immigration: that immigrants take jobs from U.S.-born workers or drive down wages. But this study — like many before it — suggests the labor market isn't that simple. It suggests that immigrants and native-born workers often don't compete against each other for the exact same jobs.

"Especially undocumented immigrants, they typically take lower-paid, more dangerous, more dirty, more seasonal, less reliable jobs," East says. And, research suggests, "employers are not able or willing to raise wages in order to attract U.S.-born workers to take those jobs."

Meanwhile, immigrant labor helps core industries operate and grow. And when immigrant workers disappear from those industries, East says, employment prospects can worsen for native-born workers too.

East gave an example from the construction sector. " If a construction company is having a really hard time finding construction site laborers because of ICE activity, they're gonna build fewer homes, they're gonna build fewer buildings in general, and they're gonna hire less in general, including hiring less U.S.-born workers," East says.

To use econ jargon, this study, like many before it, suggests that immigrants tend to complement rather than substitute for native-born workers. Again, the labor market seems to be less of a Hunger Games, and more like a potluck.

It's conceivable, however, that there are some sectors that are more zero-sum, and immigrants do displace or undercut native workers. For example, we did a two-part newsletter series on the Chinese Exclusion Acts, which was the first major immigration crackdown in U.S. history. We spoke to Nancy Qian, who co-authored a study on the effects of that crackdown on the economy. And she found that white miners, who competed with miners from China, seemed to benefit economically from exclusion. But even in Qian's study, basically everyone else suffered economically from that 19th-century immigration crackdown.

East's study focuses on the labor market, but that's only one part of the broader economic picture. Undocumented immigrants are also consumers, injecting money into the economy, and taxpayers who, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office, boost government revenue. And their labor could also help lower the price of goods and services. East says she's currently working on a study that looks at this. Undocumented immigrants make up a significant share of the labor force in industries like food service, agriculture, childcare, and construction.

One final note on this new study is it's a working paper, which means it hasn't gone through a peer-review process. That said, its findings support a much larger body of research on the effects of mass deportations.

"Whether you're studying mass deportations today, whether you're studying mass deportations in the first Obama administration, as I did before, or whether you're studying mass deportations in the 1930s, as some of my friends in economics have done, you see the same pattern of results: which is that mass deportations are not only harmful for immigrant workers themselves, but they're harmful for U.S.-born workers and the labor market more broadly," East says.

We reached out to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees immigration enforcement, to get their response to this study, which suggests that the Trump administration's immigration crackdown has had negative economic impacts. A spokesperson said: "Let's be clear, if there was any correlation between rampant illegal immigration and a good economy, Biden would have had a booming economy. Removing these criminals from the streets makes communities safer for business owners and customers."

A change of tactics

After the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, the Trump administration appeared to shift its immigration enforcement strategy — not just in Minneapolis, but nationwide.

In their analysis of ICE activity published last month, the Deportation Data Project found that enforcement nationwide fell meaningfully, "with street arrests declining to roughly their September 2025 levels." But, they wrote, "it is unclear whether this decline in enforcement will persist; appropriations from the 'One Big Beautiful Bill' will allow ICE to continue to hire more officers and expand detention capacity."

East's new study looks at the first nine months of the Trump administration. And, she says, she's now crunching the numbers on what's happened since then. On the one hand, she says, " the number of these arrests that might have the biggest chilling effects is falling."

But, on the other hand, " given the spectacle that we saw in 2025, it may be hard to sort of reverse that effect, or at least reverse that effect in any quick way," East says. "I think we'll need to investigate that in the data itself."

We will continue following this story. If you aren't already, subscribe to the Planet Money newsletter: npr.org/planetmoneynewsletter.

text:
Federal government payments to keep immigration detainees at an Indiana prison are lagging by five months, according to monthly reporting released under a new state law.

Indiana has not been paid since November, said the Department of Correction filings provided Monday to the Indiana Capital Chronicle. The state has spent about $10 million to accommodate detainees at the Miami Correctional Facility since then.

Hoosier officials agreed to a two-year contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to hold up to 1,000 detainees at a time in a previously unused wing of the prison.

Detainees sent to Miami are adult men classified as medium-maximum security for stays longer than 72 hours.

Under the agreement, which began Oct. 1 and runs through September 2027, ICE will pay Indiana $291.24 per bed per day — which DOC Commissioner Lloyd Arnold has said is about four times the $75 daily per-person cost for inmates at the prison.

The agency previously told the Capital Chronicle it had been paid $1.17 million for October and $3.86 million for November.

The DOC’s submissions to the State Budget Committee, however, list roughly $5 million in payments under November only.

The documents were filed pursuant to Senate Enrolled Act 76, a controversial immigration enforcement measure. Republicans accepted a Democratic amendment to require monthly reporting from DOC on expenses and revenue related to the ICE contract.

The provision — which took effect March 5, when the law was signed — required the agency to submit a “status update” by March 15, including money spent and received between Oct. 1 and March 1.

Future status reports are due monthly through 2027.

But the March and April reports “were mistakenly left off the April committee agenda” for the State Budget Committee, according to Department of Revenue spokeswoman Megan Kramer.

The committee is scheduled to meet Tuesday afternoon “to consider the two time-sensitive items on the agenda” — both state university campus projects on an abnormally short to-do list.

The reports show DOC has spent $12.5 million housing detainees since the contract began through March, but has received less than $5.1 million from ICE over that time period.

About $5.9 million of the expenditures were labeled “contractual services,” with $5.2 million going to”personal services and fringe benefits.”

DOC also logged spending of $646,000 on supplies, parts and materials; $382,000 on capital costs; $340,000 on utilities and $67,000 on administrative and operating expenses.

The Budget Committee previously approved almost $15.8 million in upfront costs to prepare the prison along U.S. 31 near Grissom Air Reserve Base for its stint as what Trump administration officials dubbed the “Speedway Slammer.”

The money was intended to fund a wide range of infrastructure upgrades and equipment purchases, according to committee documents.

text:
DENVER, Colorado — Kerri Calcador and Andrea Koppenhofer dedicated their professional careers to public service. Calcador was a prosecuting attorney before she became an immigration judge on the Denver bench. Koppenhoffer served as an immigration judge in both New York and Colorado after stints in state and municipal courts. Neither of them expected to step down in 2025, but they both decided to depart their posts in May 2025 - only a few months into President Trump's second term, amidst policy changes.

Since then, Calcador has begun a low-bono law firm aimed at helping immigrants access legal resources with Koppenhofer as Counsel. Asylum on a Budget with Counsel began during the fall of 2025 and has since taken on dozens of clients. They work with clients on their asylum paperwork and offer guidance on how to represent themselves in court from the perspective of an immigration judge.

They sat down for an interview with 9NEWS Reporter Angeline McCall. The transcript is below:

Question: How long were you guys on the Denver bench with immigration as an immigration judge?

Calcador: I was on the Denver bench for five years and a few months.

Koppenhofer: So I started in New York in 2020 at New York Broadway, and then I came to the Denver bench in March of 2023.

Question: You both stepped down in 2025 around May. Tell me about that decision and what led you to that.

Calcador: So in early 2025, as the administration changed, certain policies started coming down through email. One of the policies that really made me pause and think about whether this was going to impact my role as an immigration judge was a policy encouraging the immigration judges to deny asylum applications on their face without a hearing. The reason why it was important is because we have the largest percentage of pro se applicants in immigration court throughout the country. And so, for my experience with working with pro se applicants, the asylum application that's filed usually does not contain the full story of why a person left their country and what they're afraid of. So, for an application to be denied on its face without giving a person a reason or a hearing to explain their reasons why they left their country. I felt like that was not going to be fair. Applications were filed very quickly for them to get work authorization or to be filed within a one-year bar. They're in English. They're not in Spanish. So most people didn't understand what the application contained. And so that was a real concern for me going following a policy where I would deny people relief and basically order them removed without giving them a chance to meet with me and find out really why they left their country.

Koppenhofer: I think shortly after the inauguration, it may have even been the day after when I returned to the office, and there were a slew of emails with executive orders that had titles like protecting the state and the people from invasion, dismissal of dangerous DEI programs, characterizing the Dred Scott v. Sanford 1857 Supreme Court decision as shameful. I was very concerned that those were red flags to me. And then I would say, I knew that I was going to need to find a different place. I would say on January 22nd, there was a memo on January 22nd that asked employees to please report other employees who are engaging in DEI practices within 10 days or suffer adverse consequences.

Then, on April 9th, another memo came out not allowing judges to continue their association with the American Bar Association. And the importance of that is they are a leading organization for the bar and for attorneys. They file amicus briefs about changes in the law, they help lead the direction of the law and its practice, and they maintain professionalism. So being a member of that, which I was at the time, was very important to me.

And then I think, as Carrie already mentioned, when the April 11th memo came out encouraging judges to dismiss cases without a hearing, It just told me the message was clear that due process was not important here.

McCall: Did you feel like you guys still had independence as judges on the bench, or was it being more guided by these executive orders or policies?

Calcador: So I think we did have some independence. The due process requires us to follow statutes and case law. Policies are not a requirement to proceed with due process. So I think we did have some independence, but you could tell it was being slowly taken away in one way or another by increasing the demands on how many cases we were to be completing. They would put it in a calendar year, try to complete this many cases per calendar year, but when you divide it up, per how many working days you're working. At the time we were there, it was around three. It has increased exponentially since we've left. And so there were ways for them to take away our independence in other ways, other than specifically telling us, you need to rule on this particular case this way. It wasn't like that. It was more, kind of guiding us to following the procedures and policies that they were putting in place.

Koppenhofer: Yeah, I think the independence is limited. And it started in 2018, I think, with the Attorney General's order taking away administrative closure. And that's a very important tool that judges can use, particularly when they, when an applicant comes before you that may have, who's in removal proceedings, that may have more than one path to remaining here legally, and sometimes they take time. USCIS adjudicates certain paths. We hear asylum and some adjustments and some other relief from removal, but sometimes USCIS can't get to a path that's available to a person that appears before us. And we could use that tool to give them time so that they could remain here legally and pursue their path after they made all that effort and took all that risk to get here. So that's, I think, when it started.

They also instituted metrics that were being applied to judges. And as Carrie mentioned, they were completion of 700 cases per year, and fewer than 15 % of cases that were appealed returned to you. So you had to achieve those metrics. Anytime you introduce metrics or you politicize or put pressure on judges to complete cases, of course, it's going to rush due process, and that's something you don't want. You can't interpret whether the case that comes before you has issues that you need more time to either flesh out the facts on or review the law on. So I do think it's limited. I think, as Carrie said, it's gotten much worse, especially there was a June memo, I think in 2025, that came down that really criticized judges and their I think it just said they were biased against DHS, but there were no examples given. So I think that puts a lot of pressure on judges.

McCall: So it's not so much a quota, right, that judges have to meet, but it is maybe a benchmark for how many cases judges might be expected to take on daily or weekly or yearly.

Calcador: Yeah, it's like a benchmark. However, if you're a judge, you're most likely a type A personality, right? So all of us are type A. We want to hit the benchmarks. We all want to hit the benchmarks. And so to put the benchmarks out there, even if they tell us you're not going to be rated based on if you meet the benchmark. And by the way, when you look at the benchmark, it starts with you failing. So you start in the red, failing. And you have to prove yourself to get over to the green part, where you're being successful. So when you deal with a bunch of type A personalities, we want to get to successful.

So we want to hit the benchmark. However, each case, like Andrea was saying, each case is completely different. You cannot compare my docket to Andrea's docket. You can't compare. detention cases to non -detained cases. And each individual case, an asylum case, could take one hour, or it could take 16 hours, you know, that needs to be divided up over several days. I mean, every case really depends on that particular case and handling the issues that are in dispute in that one case. So it's really hard to judge how a judge is using their time.

Koppenhofer: And cases that don't have representation are going to take longer. People come into court, they're very nervous. Everything counts, right, at that moment. So it may take some time for them to become relaxed and for the judge to get them to that place so that we can elicit the facts that we need from them and not have them make any misstatements. Give them a chance to tell their story as it occurred. That's really what's important. And then we also may spot some issues along the way that they're not aware of. Maybe you engaged in some activity that we have to flesh out to see if there's a bar to your application. That takes time, and it didn't come in the application, so we don't know if that exists in that case. There's definitely that issue, and I also just want to say that I think many or all the judges probably met that quota, as Carrie said.

Judges work very, very hard, but it does put pressure on you, and they also administered, I can't remember when the last time out, in absentia orders could be issued. In absentia orders are very difficult to get overturned. So if you fail to appear, which we know is a common thing, because immigrants come here, you're a displaced person in a new area. You have to find a place to live, without money, maybe initially, or get a job. Your notices for court are being mailed to the address that you originally came in on. So that makes it very, very difficult. And it was when you're trying to meet a number in an absentia order is an easy order to give. And especially when the department asks you to give that order, and there isn't any reason not to. It was sent to the last known address.

You know, you have followed the law. So that was another way our authority was limited. Maybe in those cases, we might have given a continuance if there was some type of good cause we could find. But that was discouraged, I felt.

McCall: The quota or the benchmark, do you think it's sustainable for judges today to meet those case numbers?

Koppenhofer: Again, I think it's very difficult to say. For example, if you have languages where it's very difficult to get interpreters, so you may set those cases on a day where a MAM interpreter is not available, or you need a relay interpreter because the MAM interpreter can't speak English or can't, doesn't qualify in that, so you need a Spanish interpreter. You need someone, you need two interpreters. It's very difficult. So if you've set aside a morning for that hearing and one of the interpreters can't make it, you have lost that time to hear cases. So I think it's difficult to say if people can make them. If you have very standard cases, I had a docket with primarily Chinese immigrants when I was in New York, and that case typically is a religious case, and there's good case law on that. It's primarily credibility. And so those cases, I think you can do two or three of them in a day or four if you don't have a bar and deliver an oral decision. So it really depends on the docket. And there are a lot of languages. And finding out which language the person in front of you needs can also be difficult to do. And we're required to provide an interpreter for the language that they speak and understand best.

Calcador: By increasing the benchmark for the judges that remain at the immigration court, I think they're really put between a rock and a hard place, because the judges all want to give due process. The policies and the case law now wants the judge to deny the applications without a hearing. The benchmark's here, and if they can deny, you know, if they only finish one case today, but they can go ahead and deny 10, because those are applications that are not legally sufficient when filed, that gets them closer to the benchmark. I'm not saying that's what they want to do, but there's a pressure, you know, they're being pressured to do between the policies and their metrics.

McCall: Do you think it's harder for immigrants today to have more fair outcomes on their immigration cases because of these policies or changes?

Calcador: I do, and I always told, and I still tell my clients today they ask me can I get a fair hearing at immigration court without a lawyer, or do I really need a lawyer? And I would say when I was the immigration judge, I never felt like someone needed to have a lawyer, and I'm not their lawyer when I'm the immigration judge. I am just the neutral arbiter, but I felt like there was - all of us understood the pro se community, and we were able to get the information we needed. And as long as they knew what the qualifications were for the relief that they were seeking, we were able to get that information out of them and tell them whether they had a viable case or not. So my answer was, no, you don't need a lawyer as long as you understand the process and you know what the legal requirements are. And if you meet those legal requirements, I don't think you need a lawyer.

Now it's a little harder, because if you don't have a very well-documented case, you may fall within that sweep of cases that were improperly filed or not legally sufficient when filed. And so it's harder now for people, for sure.

Koppenhofer: There's definitely time constraints that contribute to that. The judges are not, I don't think they're able to give continuances and find good cause, maybe as they could have before. And I don't think immigrants know always how to present good cause, what good cause is. So if the facts aren't there for a judge to give a continuance or continuances are discouraged, it's going to be very difficult to give a fair trial.

If time was needed to obtain documents that we didn't know we needed or how to get, or we can't get them from our government, whereas we used to be able to do that more.

McCall: When we talk about Denver only having about 15% of defendants who have representation, what kind of impact did that do here in Denver with these policies specifically, because we know that the challenges here for people who don't have representation are different than maybe across the country?

Calcador: I think it had a much higher impact on the immigrant population here than anywhere else in the country just because there's a lack of availability for it, representation. Based on the cost and maybe not enough lawyers, I'm not sure exactly why, but it definitely hit a higher number here and especially back in early 2025 or mid 2025 when ICE was coming to the courtrooms. And they're not doing that anymore, but when they were coming to the courtrooms, it was really discouraging people from coming, showing up for court. So that really hit a harsh, large number of immigrants in Denver, I believe.

Koppenhofer: Yeah. And when you don't have representation, again, it certainly makes it easier for the judges to go through the I-589 asylum applications and deny yours without a hearing. And so, of course, that's going to make it more difficult for people to present their case here, to have an opportunity to present their case, because they don't have access to people that can help them. And also cutting the resources of some of the volunteer organizations that used to come in, because they could help them. They could inform people about gatherings they were hosting that would help them with their I -589.

So that information, also that flow of information to immigrants, went away, because they didn't have the funding to have a person at the courthouse or in the courtroom helping with that.

McCall: You two both really have dedicated your life to practicing law and being in this space. Was it difficult for you guys to walk away?

Calcador: It was very hard for me. I've been a federal employee. I was a federal employee for 29 years when I left. And I did get an early retirement. So, but it wasn't when I wanted to retire. I wasn't ready to retire yet. I was probably going to stay for at least four or five more years before retirement. And so that was tough to leave because that's all I knew. And to leave something that was very comfortable for me and that I dedicated my whole career to federal work, I walked away from opportunities for more money to have a purpose with the government to serve. And so when I left, It was hard, but I left with the notion that I was going to do something to further serve the community. And so it just took me a few months to figure it out. But, you know, I'm very happy with what I'm doing now, and that I am in, I'm still in the immigration field and I'm still able to serve the community. And I think even now in a more meaningful way.

Koppenhofer: It was very difficult. I mean, I relocated my whole family to New York to be an immigration judge, and I've been a jurist since 2011. So I planned on remaining in this position until past my retirement, and I'm not, I'm not, I haven't retired from anything yet, but that was my goal. And the bigger goal was to have an impact on this number and to be the guardian or preserver of due process because I really learned a lot serving with the jurists I worked with here in Colorado. This is truly a great state for the judiciary. They understand due process, and they want to take the steps to ensure that it's delivered here in this state, all through your initial courts, all the way up to the Supreme Court. The judges here have access to each other.

We talk about it frequently. And I really felt I could bring that to this job. So to have it cut off or thwarted before I had an opportunity to see it to fruition is really difficult for me, and I have to say I had a little difficulty for a few months figuring out my direction and what I wanted to do. so that I could still have that pursuit of having an impact. And it was great when Carrie reached out and her colleague, Amanda, who was also an interpreter at the court, so I knew her well, and said, "Why don't you join us?" And it helped me find that continued direction.

McCall: So, both of you have been really clear that you left before maybe you expected to or anticipated to. What kind of longterm impact does this do on the immigration system if other judges continue to leave because they don't want to continue to adhere to policies like this?

Calcador: I think it is going to have a very adverse long -term effect because you're losing people who have the decades of knowledge and experience because they just can't handle the pressure and stress anymore. And so that's going to cause new people to be brought in that don't have the experience and who are just going to do things possibly in an expedited fashion that's not consistent with how we want cases to be heard as adjudicators. I mean, I think it is going to have a really negative impact, in my opinion.

Koppenhofer: I agree. It will definitely have a negative impact. I mean, working in New York, I worked with jurists who'd been on the bench for 20 years, 25 years. The institutional knowledge, the wealth of that knowledge that they have is incredible. Should it be mixed with new judges and incoming judges? Of course it should. But it helps balance new ideas that have been tried before. What happens? So we can hone, maybe it's still a great idea, but we can hone it. We can change some of the approach and the procedure to it. They also uphold the rule of law. They understand the history of immigration. And it's not to say that new judges don't understand that, but they've lived it. They've created it. They've seen administrations come and go that have imposed different types of restrictions on them or given them maybe a little more authority. But they understand the evenness required under those administrations so that we're not swinging right to left with immigration. with the law that we've been given by the legislature. So I think that it really damages the rule of law to fire or discourage longevity on the bench.

McCall: Tell us about what you're doing now and how that prior experience has led you to ABC or Asylum.

Calcador: Sure. So, Asylum on a Budget with Council is a low-bono law firm that I created. I thought of the idea with Amanda Seha, which was the immigration court interpreter at the Denver court, who left at the same time that we left. And so we kind of worked on it over the summer, how we were going to create this business to help people get through this, all the changes in this administration, knowing that they can't afford a lawyer. So we do it for the very lowest cost we possibly can.

And we work with lots of organizations in the community that also help sponsor certain people who can't even make our low fee. They will come in and sponsor those people. So it's really a huge community effort at getting people some legal guidance when they can't afford a lawyer and immigration court. So we review people's applications. We strengthen their asylum applications.

We help them draft their applications in terms of their declaration, their statements. We do everything in English and also their native language because they don't know what their application says. So now they have their application in their native language, their statement in their native language. I draft a legal argument directing the adjudicator to how I believe that they qualify for asylum and that's in their native language. They have country conditions prepared for them. Basically, everything a lawyer would do is prepared for them.

And then when it comes to them going to court or to USCIS for adjudication. We bring them in, put on our robes. We're back in the judge position now, and we're practicing with them so that when they go to court, they've already done this. It's something they're familiar with, and how they answer their questions, and we guide them on that. When you answer this question, I think you should say it more this way. So when they go to court now, yes, they're unrepresented, but they're prepared.

And so it's just a whole different experience. And obviously, there's only two of us. We can't handle the entire community, but we're trying to help as many people as we can, and I think it's a good service that we provide. We just do it as low cost as we can. It's a good time to mention that the Behringer Law Firm has been so supportive of our business and they provide a space to conduct our business out of their business.

So, I mean, I want to shout out to the Behringer Law Firm that they've really helped us along because we don't even have enough money for office space, printing, and a legal assistant, and they just provide all of that to us. just to support the fact that we're helping the community, which I think is amazing. Yeah.

Koppenhofer: We were initially meeting clients at a church, and they were very gracious to allow us to meet there, but it was in a, you know, a church classroom. And sometimes there's events and singing going on. It's beautiful, but the Behringer law firm, was very gracious in providing us more than one room.

So we have a conference room. If we both have clients simultaneously, we can meet with them. And the legal assistant has been invaluable so that we can have someone regularly answering phone calls because Amanda Seha, who works with ABC and was the former interpreter at the court, that's not really her role as an administrator. She's an interpreter. And she also translates documents for us and does a Certificate of Translation, which is another thing we provide along with the completed application. Because a lot of documents will be barred from the court reviewing them if you don't have a Certificate of Translation that is clearly for that document.

So these are very important details that we know as judges can cause your entire case to blow up. And we're trying to help people be ready. And I think it's also helpful to judges when we've put these declarations into, it's not just a stream of consciousness of what happened to me. It's organized in maybe how it relates to political opinion, to their claims, how it may relate to their race, what the nexus or connection to that is. And we try to group it that way so that the judge can see what the connections are. And that will help them with this immense pressure to complete their case.

title: How to Restore Credibility, Humanity to Immigration Enforcement
description:

text:
Washington DC, May 12 Tues – Today, the American Immigration Council released a new framework calling for the overhaul of the United States’ immigration enforcement system. The framework argues that the country’s current approach is fundamentally disconnected from public safety and has trapped the immigration debate into a false binary between either mass deportation or no enforcement at all.

Restoring Credibility and Humanity: A New Framework for Immigration Enforcement, lays out a roadmap for replacing indiscriminate mass deportation with a system focused on increasing compliance with the law, prioritizing public safety threats, proportionate consequences, and meaningful accountability for government abuse.

Read the framework here.

The proposal comes amid growing backlash to the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda, which has swept in longtime residents, families, business owners, and people actively pursuing lawful status.

“Mass deportation has eroded public trust in the federal government by treating every immigrant as a violent criminal,” said Nayna Gupta, national policy director and co-author of the report. “A credible system should give people who want to follow the rules, a way to do so, and use consequences that are proportionate to the actual violation. The Trump administration has weaponized outdated laws that use detention and deportation as a one-size-fits-all punishment, even for people with long-standing ties who pose no public safety threat.”

The framework proposes major reforms across four pillars:

Creating a new process for long-term undocumented residents to gain lawful permanent status through fines, community service, and probation-like systems instead of deportation.

Revising outdated laws to focus enforcement on people convicted of violent or especially serious recent crimes while professionalizing enforcement.

Legislating new, proportionate consequences for violations of immigration law, rather than subjecting every immigration violator to detention and deportation.

Establishing independent oversight and stronger court authority to hold immigration agencies and agents accountable for abuses.

The framework argues that immigration enforcement should be measured not by the number of deportations carried out, but by whether laws are enforced consistently, fairly, and humanely.

“The whole goal when all this immigration stuff started ramping up about a year and a half ago was to get violent offenders off the street. And no one has any problem with that. The issue is you have people who are here and they are following the rules—people who are reporting to their regular check-ins and being taken into custody at those check-ins. Things like that really erode trust and really make it more dangerous for everyone out here when law enforcement can’t be trusted,” said Joseph Kennedy, sheriff of Dubuque county, Iowa.

The framework also calls for sweeping accountability reforms, asserting that public confidence in immigration enforcement cannot be rebuilt without meaningful oversight and consequences for abuses of power. That means that agencies and agents that abuse their power should be reined in or pushed out. Among other recommendations, the proposal calls for expanding judicial authority to review unlawful enforcement actions, creating an independent immigration accountability commission, strengthening internal oversight offices within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and giving victims of civil rights violations the ability to sue.

“Building a credible and humane immigration enforcement system depends on establishing that enforcement agencies are accountable both to the public and other branches of government,” said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, senior fellow and co-author of the report. “No law enforcement agency can maintain legitimacy if abuses of power carry no consequences. A credible enforcement system must give courts and Congress stronger authority to intervene when federal agencies and officers abuse their authority.”

The framework warns that the U.S. has reached a critical point after decades of failed immigration policymaking that is overly focused on punishment instead of long-term compliance and public safety. According to the report, continuing down the path of indiscriminate enforcement risks locking the country into a permanent system of mass detention and social disruption.

“We are facing a choice between indiscriminate enforcement that destabilizes communities and pulls resources away from genuine public safety threats, versus credible enforcement that is targeted, proportional, and actually capable of delivering public safety,” said Gupta. “The question is not whether immigration laws should be enforced. The question is whether enforcement will be smart, focused, and humane, or driven by fear, quotas, and political theater.”

"HB9 and the SCPO unlawfully interfere with federal immigration enforcement, illegally discriminate against federal operations, and violate constitutional protections regarding contracts and federal supremacy.

text:
The federal government is suing New Mexico over a state law that prohibits counties and local law enforcement from assisting federal agents in enforcing immigration laws.

On Friday, the federal government filed a complaint and motion for preliminary injunction against the State of New Mexico, NM Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham, NM Attorney General Raul Torrez, the City of Albuquerque and Albuquerque Mayor Timothy Keller, alleging that House Bill 9 and an Albuquerque city ordinance are keeping the federal immigration system from running the way that Congress and the Constitution intended.

"New Mexico is attempting to regulate immigration policy, something the federal government is clearly and uniquely empowered by the Constitution to do," said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. "Our filings seek to halt the state’s unconstitutional actions by preserving cooperation between federal, state, and local law enforcement and allowing federal immigration officials to enforce the law."

RELATED: New Mexico governor signs Immigrant Safety Act among other bills into law

HB 9, entitled "Immigration Safety Act," stops any public body, such as any state or local government, sheriff's department, commission, etc., from partnering with federal agencies to detain people suspected of breaking immigration laws and keeps federal agents from using public property to detain people.

While the Albuquerque City Ordinance O-26-15, entitled "Safe Community Places Ordinance (SCPO)," prohibits the use of city property for immigration enforcement and also asks employers to inform their employees when an immigration agency is going to inspect their business.

"The State of New Mexico and the City of Albuquerque seek to intentionally obstruct federal law enforcement by preventing cooperation between local governments and the federal government," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison for the District of New Mexico. "HB9 and the SCPO unlawfully interfere with federal immigration enforcement, illegally discriminate against federal operations, and violate constitutional protections regarding contracts and federal supremacy. Additionally, by barring public entities from participating in federal immigration detention in New Mexico, HB9 jeopardizes nearly 300 jobs and the economy of Otero County. Our lawsuit asks the court to declare these laws invalid and issue an immediate injunction to stop them from being enforced."

Meanwhile, NM Attorney General Raul Torrez issued the following statement, saying that under the Constitution, states have the authority to enforce their laws and his office stands by them:

House Bill 9 is a constitutional exercise of state authority, and this office will defend it.

The New Mexico Legislature passed this law after extensive consideration of documented harms occurring in immigration detention facilities operating in this state — inadequate medical care, deaths in custody, and conditions that fell well below acceptable standards. The Legislature made a considered judgment that New Mexico's government, its employees, and its publicly funded facilities should not be instruments of a detention system that has caused serious and preventable harm to people held within our borders. That is precisely the kind of policy judgment that belongs to the states.

The Constitution reserves to the states the power to govern their own affairs — including how state and local personnel are deployed and how publicly funded facilities are used. Federal agents remain free to enforce federal immigration law. They may make arrests, conduct investigations, and carry out removals. What they may not do is compel New Mexico's officers, employees, and institutions to administer federal enforcement priorities the state has chosen not to adopt. The federal government has its own personnel and its own resources. It does not have a constitutional right to New Mexico's.

This lawsuit asks a federal court to override a democratically enacted state law because the administration disagrees with the policy choice the Legislature made. That is not a constitutional argument. It is an attempt to use federal litigation to reverse an outcome the administration dislikes. We will see them in court.
